label: def:wk_decompose
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:wk_decompose}
    We say a permutation $w$ is \textbf{left-weakly decomposable} in $\operatorname{\mathfrak{S}}_n$ if there exists an integer $1\leq i< n-1$ such that
    \[\{w(1),\ldots, w(i)\}\subseteq [i+1].\]
    A permutation $w$ is \textbf{weakly decomposable} if either $w$ or $w^{-1}$ is left-weakly decomposable.  
    If $w$ is not weakly decomposable, we say that $w$ is \textbf{strongly indecomposable}.
head: environment

label: lem:wk_decomposable_support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:wk_decomposable_support}
A permutation $w$ is left-weakly decomposable in $\operatorname{\mathfrak{S}}_n$ if and only if there exist $1\leq i<n-1$ and a unique decomposition $w=w_1\cdot w_2$ such that $S(w_1)\subseteq [i]$ and $S(w_2)\subseteq [n-1]\setminus [i]$.

label: lem:wk_decomposable_patterns
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:wk_decomposable_patterns}
Let $w=w_1\cdot w_2$ be a weakly decomposing factorization in $\operatorname{\mathfrak{S}}_n$.  If $p$ is strongly indecomposable in $\operatorname{\mathfrak{S}}_r$ for some $r\leq n$, then $w$ avoids $p$ if and only if $w_1$ and $w_2$ avoid $p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First note that $p$ is strongly indecomposable if and only if $p^{-1}$ is strongly indecomposable.  Moreover, $w$ contains $p$ if and only if $w^{-1}$ contains $p^{-1}$.  Hence, without loss of generality, we may assume that $w$ is left-weakly decomposable.  
    
    Let $w=w_1\cdot w_2$ is a left-weakly decomposing factorization such that $S(w_1)\subseteq [i]$ and $S(w_2)\subseteq[n]\setminus[i]$.  Suppose $w$ avoids $p$.  For the sake of contradiction, if $w_1$ contains $p$, then any containment of $p$ must be within the sequence $w_1(1)\cdots w_1(i+1)$ since $w_1(k)=k$ for $k>i+1$ and $p$ is strongly indecomposable.  But $w$ contains the sequence $w_1(1)\cdots w_1(i+1)$ and hence would also contain $p,$ which is a contradiction.  Thus $w_1$ avoids $p$.  By a similar argument, $w_2$ also avoids $p$.  

    Conversely, assume that $w_1$ and $w_2$ each avoid $p$ and suppose that $w$ contains $p$.  If $p$ is contained within $w(1)\cdots w(i)$, then $w_1$ would contain $p$.  Similarly, if $p$ is contained within $w(i+1)\cdots w(n)$, then $w_2$ would contain $p$. Hence any containment of $p$ within $w$ must involve entries before and after $w(i+1)$ in one-line notation.
    
    Let $p=p(1)\cdots p(r)$ and fix a containment of $p$ within $w$.   Let $p(1)\cdots p(r')$ denote the sequence entries contained within $w(1)\cdots w(i)$.  Note that this sequence is non-empty and $r'<r$.     
    Since $\{w(1),\ldots, w(i)\}\subseteq [i+1]$, we must have $\{p(1),\ldots,p(r')\}\subseteq [r'+1]$.  This implies that $p$ is left-weakly decomposable, which is a contradiction.  Thus $w$ must avoid $p$.
head: environment

label: def:staircase
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:staircase}  Let $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ be a set of non-empty intervals in $[n-1]$ where $B_i=[l_i,r_i]$ and
\[\text{$l_i<l_{i+1}$ and $r_i<r_{i+1}$  for all  $i$.}\]
We say a partial order $\preceq$ on $ \mathcal{D}$ is a \textbf{staircase diagram} on $[n-1]$ if the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $(B_i,B_j)$ is a cover relation if and only if $j=i\pm 1$ and $B_i\cup B_j$ is connected.
\item If $B_{i-1}\succ B_i\prec B_{i-1}$ or $B_{i-1}\prec B_i\succ B_{i+1}$, then $B_{i-1}\cup B_{i+1}$ is disconnected.
\end{enumerate}
We also include $\mathcal{D}=\varnothing$ as the empty staircase diagram.

label: thm:smooth_bijection
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:smooth_bijection}
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a staircase diagram on $[n-1]$.  Then the permutation $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ is well-defined.
Furthermore, the map $\Lambda$ is a bijection:
$$\{\text{Staircase diagrams on $[n-1]$}\}\xrightarrow{\Lambda} \{w\in \operatorname{\mathfrak{S}}_n\ |\ w\text{ is smooth}\}.$$
head: environment

label: prop:staircase_permutation_properties
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: prop:staircase_wk_decomp
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the proposition by induction on $k=|\mathcal{D}|$. If $k=2$, then $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,B_2\}$ with $B_1\cap B_{2}=\varnothing$. If $B_1\cup B_{2}$ is disconnected, then $B_1$ and $B_2$ are both maximal (and minimal) in $\mathcal{D}$.  Thus
$$\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=u_{B_2}\cdot u_{J(B_2)}\cdot \Lambda(\{B_1\})=u_{B_1}\cdot u_{J(B_1)}\cdot \Lambda(\{B_2\}).$$
Since $B_1\cap B_{2}=\varnothing$, we have $u_{J(B_1)}=u_{J(B_2)}=\text{id}$ and hence
$$\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=\Lambda(\{B_1\})\cdot \Lambda(\{B_2\})=\Lambda(\{B_2\})\cdot \Lambda(\{B_1\}).$$  
If $B_1\prec B_{2}$, then only $B_2$ is maximal in $\mathcal{D}$ and
$$\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=u_{B_2}\cdot u_{J(B_2)}\cdot \Lambda(\{B_1\})=\Lambda(\{B_2\})\cdot \Lambda(\{B_1\}).$$
Similarly, if $B_1\succ B_{2}$, then only $B_1$ is maximal and $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=\Lambda(\{B_1\})\cdot \Lambda(\{B_2\})$.

Now suppose $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots, B_k\}$ with $B_i\cap B_{i+1}=\varnothing$ for some $i<k$.  If $B_i\cup B_{i+1}$ is disconnected, then the blocks in $\mathcal{D}_1$ and $\mathcal{D}_2$ are pairwise incomparable in $\mathcal{D}$ and hence both sets contain a block that is maximal in $\mathcal{D}$.  Let $B_m$ be maximal in $\mathcal{D}$ such that $m\leq i$.  By induction, 
$$\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=u_{B_m}\cdot u_{J(B_m)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}\setminus\{B_m\})=u_{B_m}\cdot u_{J(B_m)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1\setminus\{B_m\})\cdot\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2).$$
Since $B_m\cap S(\mathcal{D}_2)=\varnothing$, the set $J(B_m)$ is unchanged when restricting from $\mathcal{D}$ to $\mathcal{D}_1$.  Thus  
$$u_{B_m}\cdot u_{J(B_m)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1\setminus\{B_m\})=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1).$$
A similar argument shows that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2)\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1)$ by choosing a maximal block in $\mathcal{D}_2$.

If $B_i\prec B_{i+1}$, then there exists a maximal element $B_m\in \mathcal{D}$ such that $m>i$.  If $m>i+1$, then $B_i\prec B_{i+1}$ in $\mathcal{D}\setminus\{B_m\}$.
Induction on $k$ yields 
$$\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=u_{B_m}\cdot u_{J(B_m)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}\setminus\{B_m\})=u_{B_m}\cdot u_{J(B_m)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2\setminus\{B_m\})\cdot\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1)=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2)\cdot\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1).$$
If $m=i+1$, then either $B_i\cup B_{i+2}$ is disconnected in $\mathcal{D}\setminus\{B_m\}$ or $\mathcal{D}_2=\{B_m\}$.  In either case, we still conclude $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2)\cdot\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1).$  Note that if $B_i\succ B_{i+1}$, then an analogous argument shows that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1)\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2)$.

Finally, observe that if $B_i=[l_i,r_i]$ and $B_{i+1}=[l_{i+1},r_{i+1}]$, then $$S(\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1))\subseteq [1,r_i]\quad \text{and}\quad S(\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2))\subseteq [l_{i+1},n-1].$$  Since $B_i\cap B_{i+1}=\varnothing$, we have $r_i<l_{i+1}$.  \Cref{lem:wk_decomposable_support} implies the product  $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_i)\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}_{3-i})$ is a weakly decomposing factorization for $i=1,2$.  Furthermore, if $B_i\cup B_{i+1}$ is disconnected, then \Cref{lem:decomposable} implies the product is a decomposing factorization.  This completes the proof.

label: prop:staircase_wk_decomp2
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ is left-weakly decomposable with a decomposing factorization $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=w_1\cdot w_2$.  Since the smooth patterns 3412 and 4231 are both strongly indecompsoable, it follows from \Cref{lem:wk_decomposable_patterns} that $w_1$ and $w_2$ are both smooth permutations since $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ is smooth. \Cref{thm:smooth_bijection} implies there exist staircase diagrams $\mathcal{D}_1$ on $[j-1]$ and $\mathcal{D}_2$ on $[j,n-1],$ where $w_1=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1)$ and $w_2=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2)$.  Let 
\[\mathcal{D}_1=\{B'_1,\ldots, B'_i\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{D}_2=\{B'_{i+1},\ldots, B'_{\ell}\}\]
and define 
\[\mathcal{D}'=\{B'_1,\ldots,B'_i,B'_{i+1},\ldots,B'_{\ell}\}\] with the staircase poset structures of $\mathcal{D}_1 $ and $\mathcal{D}_2$, and with the additional relation $B'_i\succ B'_{i+1}$ if $B'_i\cup B'_{i+1}$ is connected.  Since $B'_i\cap B'_{i+1}=\varnothing$, we have
\[\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=w_1\cdot w_2=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_1)\cdot\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_2)=\Lambda(\mathcal{D}').\]
But \Cref{thm:smooth_bijection} implies that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ uniquely determines $\mathcal{D}$ and hence $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}'$ and $B_i\cap B_{i+1}=\varnothing$.  If $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ is right-weakly decomposable, a similar argument applies with the same conclusion.  If $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ is decomposable, again the argument gives the same conclusion, but with $B_i\cup B_{i+1}$ disconnected.

label: lem:containment_expand
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $B_k$ is the terminal block of $\mathcal{D}$, it is either maximal or minimal. Suppose that $B_k$ is maximal.  Since $\mathcal{D}\setminus\{B_k\}=\mathcal{D}^+\setminus\{B'_k\}$ and $J(B_k)=J(B'_k)$, we have 
 $$\Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+)=u_{B'_k}\cdot u_{J(B'_k)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+\setminus\{B_k\})=u_{B'_k}\cdot u_{(B_k)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}).$$
Observe that $u_{B'_k}\cdot u_{B_k}=s_m\cdots s_n$ is a cyclic permutation whose left action appends $n+1$ to $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ and then shifts the values $(m,m+1,\ldots, n,n+1)$.  Specifically, if $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=w(1)\cdots w(n)$ in one-line notation, then $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+)=w'(1)\cdots w'(n+1)$ where 
$$w'(i)=\begin{cases}
          w(i) &\text{if  $w(i)<m$}\\
          w(i)+1 &\text{if  $m\leq w(i)\leq n$}\\
          m &\text{if  $i=n+1$.}
      \end{cases}$$
Hence $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+)$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$.
If $B_k$ is minimal in $\mathcal{D}$, then it is maximal in the dual staircase diagram $\mathcal{D}^*$.   \Cref{prop:staircase_permutation_properties} part (4) implies that
 $$\Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+)^{-1}=s_m\cdots s_n\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D})^{-1}$$ and hence
  $$\Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+)=\Lambda(\mathcal{D})\cdot s_n\cdots s_m.$$
  The right action of the cyclic shift $s_n\cdots s_m$ ``inserts" $n+1$ into the $m$-th position of $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$.  In other words,
  $$\Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+)=w(1)\cdots w(m-1)\ (n+1)\ w(m+1)\cdots  w(n)$$
  where $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}):=w(1)\cdots w(n)$.  Again we have $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}^+)$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$.

label: lem:containment_delete
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:containment_delete}
    Let $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots, B_k\}$ be a staircase diagram on $[n]$ and consider the subdiagram $\mathcal{D}'=\mathcal{D}\setminus\{B_k\}$.  Then $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{lem:containment_expand}, we can assume, without loss of generality, that $S(\mathcal{D})=[n]$ and $S(\mathcal{D}')=[n-1]$.  If $B_k$ is maximal in $\mathcal{D}$, then 
$$\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=u_{B_k}\cdot u_{J(B_k)}\cdot \Lambda(\mathcal{D}').$$

If $B_k=[m,n]$, then $J(B_k)=[m,n-1]$ and $u_{B_k}\cdot u_{J(B_k)}=s_m\cdots s_n$ is a cyclic permutation whose left action on $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$ appends $n+1$ and then shifts the values $(m,m+1,\dots, n+1)$.  We conclude that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$.

If  $B_k$ is minimal in $\mathcal{D}$, then we can again conclude that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$ by considering the dual staircase diagram $\mathcal{D}^*$ as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:containment_expand}.

label: lem:chain_containment
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:chain_containment}
Let $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ be a strongly connected, increasing chain on $[n-1]$ where $B_i=[r_i,l_i]$ for each $1\leq i\leq k$.  If $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})=w(1)\cdots w(n)$, then the subsequence $$w(1)w(2)w(l_1+1)w(l_2+1)\cdots w(l_k+1)$$ is a containment of pattern $(k+2)(k+1)12\cdots k$ in $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$.  In particular, $$\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h_k^+)=(k+2)(k+1)12\cdots k.$$ 

Furthermore, by duality (i.e. \Cref{prop:staircase_permutation_properties} part (4)), if $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ is a strongly connected, decreasing chain, then $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains 
$$\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h_k^-)=\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h_k^+)^{-1}=34\cdots(k+1)(k+2) 21.$$

label: lem:chain_avoid_2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:chain_avoid_2}
Let $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ be a strongly connected staircase diagram and let $1< d\leq k$ and $\ell\geq 1$.  Define the subdiagrams 
$$\mathcal{D}'=\{B_1,\ldots, B_{d-1}\}\quad\text{and}\quad  \mathcal{D}''=\{B_d,\ldots,B_k\}.$$
Suppose that $B_d$ is maximal in $\mathcal{D}$ and that $\mathcal{D}''$ is a decreasing chain.  If $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^{-}_\ell)$, then either $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^{-}_{\ell})$ or  $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}'')$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^{-}_{\ell})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ be a staircase diagram and suppose that $\mathcal{D}$ contains a strongly connected $\ell$-chain.  By \Cref{prop:subdiagram_containment} and \Cref{lem:chain_containment}, if the chain is increasing, then $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^+_\ell)$, and if the chain is decreasing, then $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^-_\ell)$.   

Conversely, suppose that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^-_\ell)$.  We will show that $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ contains a decreasing $\ell$-chain by induction on the number of decreasing runs in $\mathcal{D}$.   Since $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^{-}_\ell)$ is strongly indecomposable, it suffices to assume $\mathcal{D}$ is a strongly connected staircase diagram by \Cref{lem:wk_decomposable_patterns} and \Cref{prop:staircase_wk_decomp}.    First, suppose that $\mathcal{D}$ is a single decreasing chain.  If $k<\ell$, then repeated applications of \Cref{lem:chain_avoid_1} imply that $\Lambda(\{B_1\})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^-_2)=4312$ which is a contradiction.  Hence $k\geq \ell$ and $\mathcal{D}$ contains a decreasing $\ell$-chain.  

If $\mathcal{D}$ is not a decreasing chain, then let $B_d$ denote the maximal block in $\mathcal{D}$ with largest index and consider the subdiagrams $\mathcal{D}':=\{B_1,\ldots,B_{d-1}\}$ and $\mathcal{D}'':=\{B_d,\ldots,B_k\}$.  In particular, $\mathcal{D}''$ is a decreasing chain.  Since $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^-_\ell)$, \Cref{lem:chain_avoid_2} implies at least one of $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$ or $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}'')$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^-_\ell)$.  If $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}'')$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^-_\ell)$, then $\mathcal{D}''$ must be a decreasing chain of at least $\ell$ blocks and hence $\mathcal{D}$ contains a decreasing $\ell$-chain.  Otherwise, $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^-_\ell)$ and, by induction, the subdiagram $\mathcal{D}'$ contains a decreasing $\ell$-chain.  In either case, $\mathcal{D}$ contains a decreasing $\ell$-chain.

Finally, if $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ contains $\Lambda(\mathcal{C}h^+_\ell)$, then $\mathcal{D}$ contains an increasing $\ell$-chain by \Cref{prop:staircase_permutation_properties} part (4) and the preceding arguments.  This proves the theorem.

title: Lemma

\label{lem:chain-indecomp-smooth}
    Let $p$ be smooth permutation with $p=\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$.  If $p$ is chain indecomposable, then $\mathcal{D}$ is a strongly connected chain.  As a consequence, $p$ is strongly indecomposable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $p$ is chain indecomposable and $p$ contains itself, there exists a strongly connected chain $\mathcal{D}'\subseteq \mathcal{D}$ such that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$ contains $p=\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$.  But $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ cannot contain a permutation of a staircase diagram with strictly smaller support. Hence $\mathcal{D}'=\mathcal{D}$.

label: prop:broken_decomposition
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:broken_decomposition}
    Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a strongly connected staircase diagram and let $p$ be a chain indecomposable permutation.  Consider the decomposition $\mathcal{D}\mapsto (\mathcal{E}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{E}_K)$ as above.  Then $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ avoids $p$ if and only if $\mathcal{E}_i$ avoids $p$ for each $1\leq i \leq K$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{D}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{D}_K$ denote the maximal chains of $\mathcal{D}$ corresponding to $\mathcal{E}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{E}_K$.  If $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ avoid $p$, then each of $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_i)$ must avoid $p$ by \Cref{prop:subdiagram_containment}.  Using \Cref{lem:containment_expand} and the assumption that $p$ is chain indecomposable, it follows that each of the corresponding broken staircases $\mathcal{E}_i$ avoids $p$.

Conversely, suppose that each $\mathcal{E}_i$ avoids $p$.  Since $\mathcal{D}_i\in \mathcal{F}r^{-1}(\mathcal{B}r^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_i))$, we get that the permutation $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}_i)$ avoids $p$.  This implies $\Lambda(\mathcal{D}')$ avoids $p$ for every chain $\mathcal{D}'\subseteq\mathcal{D}$ since each chain in $\mathcal{D}$ is in some maximal $\mathcal{D}_i$.  Again, since $p$ in chain indecomposable, we have that $\Lambda(\mathcal{D})$ avoids $p$.

label: eqn:broken_decomposition
title: Proof
body_md:
First note that since $Q$ is inverse invariant, we have $z^+_n=z^-_n$ where $z^-_n$ denotes the analogous number of strongly connected decreasing chains which avoid $Q$.  Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote a fully supported, strongly connected staircase diagram on $[n]$.  Then either $\mathcal{D}$ is a chain (increasing or decreasing), or $\mathcal{D}$ decomposes as $(\mathcal{E}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{E}_K)$ as in \Cref{prop:broken_decomposition} with $K\geq 2$.  Let $z_k^b$ denote the number of increasing broken staircases on $[k]$ that avoid $Q$. Since $Q$ is inverse invariant, $z_k^b$ also equals the number of decreasing broken staircases on $[k]$ that avoid $Q$. By \Cref{prop:broken_decomposition}, we have that 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:broken_decomposition}
\bar z_n=(2z^+_n-1)+\sum_{k=2}^{n-3}z_k^b\cdot (\bar z_{n-k}-1).
\end{equation}
Observe that the bounds on the sum above come from the fact that broken staircases have minimum support size $k=2$ and that the staircase diagram $\mathcal{E}_K$ must have at least two blocks and hence $n-k\geq 3$.  Next, we claim that $z_k^b=z^+_{k+1}-z^{+}_k$.
Let $\mathcal{D}'=\{B_1,\ldots, B_{k}\}$ be a fully supported increasing chain on $[k+1]$ and define 
\[\phi(\mathcal{D}'):=\{B_1,\ldots, B_{k-1}, B_{k}\setminus\{k+1\}\}.\]
Either $\phi(\mathcal{D}')$ is a broken staircase on $[k]$, or a strongly connected chain on $[k]$.  Moreover the map $\phi$ is a bijection from increasing chains on $[k+1]$ to the disjoint union of increasing broken staircases and increasing chains on $[k]$.  Thus the claim is proved.
Now \Cref{eqn:broken_decomposition} becomes 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:broken_decomposition2}
\bar z_n=(2z^+_n-1)+\sum_{k=2}^{n-3}(z^+_{k+1}-z^{+}_k)\cdot (\bar z_{n-k}-1)
\end{equation} and thus
\[\overline{Z}(x)=\left(2Z^+(x)-\frac{x}{1-x}\right)+\left(\frac{(1-x)Z^+(x)-x}{x}\right)\cdot\left(\overline{Z}(x)-\frac{x}{1-x}\right).\]
Solving for $\overline{Z}(x)$ proves the theorem.

label: prop:Narayana
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Narayana}
Fix $\ell\geq 2$ and let $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ be a fully supported, strongly connected increasing chain on $[n]$.  Then $\mathcal{D}$ avoids $Q_{B,\ell}$ if and only if $\operatorname{DyckP}(\mathcal{D})$ has at most $\ell-1$ peaks and the height of each valley is at least one.
In particular, \[b^+_{\ell,n}=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1} N(i,n-1)\]
where $\displaystyle N(n,i)=\frac{1}{i}\binom{n}{i}\binom{n}{i-1}$ is the $(n,i)$-Narayana number.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The Narayana number $N(n,i)$ counts the number of Dyck paths on $n$ with exactly $i$ peaks.  The proposition follows from \Cref{lem:Dyck_height_valleys} and \Cref{prop:counting_fs_inc_Catalan}.

label: cor:chain_rational
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:chain_rational}
    For $\ell\geq 2$, the generating function for the number of smooth permutations avoiding $Q_{B,\ell}$ is  rational.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{cor:GF_summary} and \Cref{prop:Narayana}, it suffices to show that the generating function $\sum_{n\geq i} N(i,n)\, x^n$ is rational for a fixed integer $i$.  However, it is known that 
    \[\sum_{n\geq i} N(n,i)\, x^n=\frac{x^i\sum_{j=1}^i N(i,j)\, x^{j-1}}{(1-x)^{2i-1}}.\]  
    This formula is stated in \cite[Example 40]{Ba06} (see also \cite[Lemma 3.3]{GAO2016}).  We remark that the sum in the numerator is called the $i$-th Narayana polynomial.

label: prop:bounded_valleys
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bounded_valleys}
Fix $q\geq 2$ and let $\mathcal{D}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}$ be a fully supported, strongly connected increasing chain on $[n]$.  Then $\mathcal{D}$ avoids $Q_{C,q}$ if and only if $\operatorname{DyckP}(\mathcal{D})$ the height of each valley is at least one and less than $q$.  In particular,
\[c^+_{q,n}=f_{q-1,n-1}\]
where $f_{q,n}$ is the number of Dyck paths on $n$ whose valley heights are less than $q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The proposition follows from \Cref{lem:Dyck_height_valleys} and \Cref{prop:counting_fs_inc_Catalan}.

label: cor:overlap_rational
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:overlap_rational}
    For $q\geq 2$, the generating function for the number of smooth permutations avoiding $Q_{C,q}$ is rational.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The corollary follows directly from techniques developed in \cite{EZ20}, but we include a proof for completeness.  Let $f_{q,n}$ denote the number of Dyck paths on $n$ whose valley heights are less than $q$ and define
\[F_q(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0} f_{q,n}\, x^n.\]
It suffices to show that $F_q(x)$ is rational for all $q\geq 2$.  First note that when $q=2$, then $F_2(x)$ is rational by \Cref{prop:bounded_valleys} and \Cref{prop:C_calc}.  We proceed by induction on $q$.  Let $P$ denote a Dyck path whose valley heights are less than $q$.  Split $P$ into $P_1$ and $P_2$ at the first occurrence, which $P$ returns to the $x$-axis.  We can write 
\[P=P_1P_2=(UP_1'D) P_2.\]
Note that $P_1'$ is Dyck path whose valley heights are less than $q-1$, while $P_2$ is a Dyck path whose valley heights are still less than $q$.  This gives 
\[f_{q,n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}f_{q-1,k}\cdot f_{q,n-k-1}\] which implies
\[F_q(x)=1+xF_{q-1}(x)\cdot F_q(x)\quad \text{and}\quad F_q(x)=\frac{1}{1-xF_{q-1}(x)}.\]
By induction, $F_q(x)$ is rational for all $q\geq 2$.
